questions.topicName: Obstructive and Restrictive Lung Diseases: Foundations and Frameworks
questions.stem: These spirometry volume-versus-time tracings compare three patterns. In the middle tracing the exhaled volume rises slowly and the one-second mark is markedly reduced relative to the total. This pattern indicates which physiology?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Restrictive defect with preserved FEV1/FVC ratio

choices.label: D
choices.text: Obstructive ventilatory defect with reduced FEV1/FVC ratio

explanation.summary: In obstructive disease, expiratory airflow is limited so FEV1 falls disproportionately to FVC, lowering the FEV1/FVC ratio and producing the slow-rising curve shown; restrictive disease instead reduces all volumes while preserving the ratio.
explanation.whyCorrect: In obstructive disease, expiratory airflow is limited so FEV1 falls disproportionately to FVC, lowering the FEV1/FVC ratio and producing the slow-rising curve shown; restrictive disease instead reduces all volumes while preserving the ratio.

questions.topicName: Obstructive and Restrictive Lung Diseases: Foundations and Frameworks
questions.stem: These flow-volume loops compare three patterns against total lung capacity and residual volume. The middle loop is shifted toward higher lung volumes with a scooped (concave) expiratory limb. Which condition does this represent?

explanation.summary: Obstructive disease shifts the loop leftward toward higher volumes (air trapping, increased RV/TLC) and produces a concave, coved expiratory limb from airflow limitation; restrictive disease instead shifts the loop rightward with reduced overall volumes.
explanation.whyCorrect: Obstructive disease shifts the loop leftward toward higher volumes (air trapping, increased RV/TLC) and produces a concave, coved expiratory limb from airflow limitation; restrictive disease instead shifts the loop rightward with reduced overall volumes.

explanation.summary: Digital clubbing reflects distal phalangeal soft-tissue proliferation and loss of the Lovibond angle; it is strongly linked to chronic hypoxemia and intrathoracic disease such as lung malignancy, bronchiectasis, and pulmonary fibrosis.

questions.topicName: Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease Part 1: Pathophysiology
questions.stem: Compared with normal lung, the emphysematous lung on the right shows abnormally enlarged airspaces. This enlargement results from destruction of what?

explanation.summary: Emphysema is defined by permanent enlargement of airspaces distal to the terminal bronchiole due to destruction of alveolar walls without significant fibrosis. Loss of septa reduces gas-exchange surface area and elastic recoil, causing airflow limitation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Emphysema is defined by permanent enlargement of airspaces distal to the terminal bronchiole due to destruction of alveolar walls without significant fibrosis. Loss of septa reduces gas-exchange surface area and elastic recoil, causing airflow limitation.

questions.topicName: Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease Part 1: Pathophysiology
questions.stem: These hepatocytes contain PAS-positive, diastase-resistant globules of misfolded protein that is deficient in the serum. Through what mechanism does this deficiency lead to emphysema in the lung?

choices.label: A
choices.text: IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation causes bronchoconstriction

choices.label: C
choices.text: Excess collagen deposition stiffens the alveolar walls

choices.label: E
choices.text: Unopposed neutrophil elastase destroys alveolar elastin

explanation.summary: Alpha-1 antitrypsin normally inhibits neutrophil elastase. When the protein misfolds and is retained in hepatocytes, serum levels fall, leaving elastase unopposed to degrade alveolar elastic tissue, producing panacinar emphysema (accelerated by smoking).
explanation.whyCorrect: Alpha-1 antitrypsin normally inhibits neutrophil elastase. When the protein misfolds and is retained in hepatocytes, serum levels fall, leaving elastase unopposed to degrade alveolar elastic tissue, producing panacinar emphysema (accelerated by smoking).

questions.topicName: Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease Part 1: Pathophysiology
questions.stem: This chest CT shows extensive low-attenuation air-filled spaces and large (>1 cm) subpleural cystic areas replacing normal lung parenchyma. These findings are characteristic of which condition?

explanation.summary: Areas of destroyed lung appear as low-attenuation regions, and thin-walled spaces larger than 1 cm are bullae. This pattern of parenchymal destruction is typical of emphysema, in contrast to the reticulation of fibrosis or airspace filling of pneumonia and edema.
explanation.whyCorrect: Areas of destroyed lung appear as low-attenuation regions, and thin-walled spaces larger than 1 cm are bullae. This pattern of parenchymal destruction is typical of emphysema, in contrast to the reticulation of fibrosis or airspace filling of pneumonia and edema.

questions.topicName: Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease Part 1: Pathophysiology
questions.stem: This diagram contrasts patterns of emphysema within the acinus. Which pattern preferentially destroys the respiratory bronchioles in an upper-lobe predominant distribution and is most strongly linked to cigarette smoking?

explanation.summary: Centriacinar emphysema damages the central portion of the acinus (respiratory bronchioles) while sparing distal alveoli, is upper-lobe predominant, and is the classic smoking-related pattern. Panacinar emphysema, associated with alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, destroys the entire acinus and is lower-lobe predominant.
explanation.whyCorrect: Centriacinar emphysema damages the central portion of the acinus (respiratory bronchioles) while sparing distal alveoli, is upper-lobe predominant, and is the classic smoking-related pattern. Panacinar emphysema, associated with alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, destroys the entire acinus and is lower-lobe predominant.

questions.topicName: Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease Part 1: Pathophysiology
questions.stem: This gross lung section shows uniform destruction throughout the entire acinus (panacinar pattern) with dilated airways. This distribution of emphysema is most strongly associated with what?

explanation.summary: Panacinar emphysema destroys the acinus uniformly and is lower-lobe predominant, the classic pattern of alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency. Smoking-related disease is instead typically centriacinar and upper-lobe predominant.
explanation.whyCorrect: Panacinar emphysema destroys the acinus uniformly and is lower-lobe predominant, the classic pattern of alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency. Smoking-related disease is instead typically centriacinar and upper-lobe predominant.

questions.topicName: Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease Part 1: Pathophysiology
questions.stem: This airway biopsy from a chronic smoker shows the normal pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium replaced by a multilayered flat epithelium (arrow). What adaptive change is depicted?

explanation.summary: Chronic irritation from cigarette smoke drives replacement of the delicate respiratory epithelium by more resistant stratified squamous epithelium, a reversible adaptive metaplasia. It compromises mucociliary clearance and can be a precursor field for dysplasia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Chronic irritation from cigarette smoke drives replacement of the delicate respiratory epithelium by more resistant stratified squamous epithelium, a reversible adaptive metaplasia. It compromises mucociliary clearance and can be a precursor field for dysplasia.

questions.topicName: Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease Part 1: Pathophysiology
questions.stem: Panel B shows an older patient with a markedly increased anteroposterior chest diameter compared with panel A. What underlies this 'barrel chest' seen in advanced COPD?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Chronic lung hyperinflation and air trapping

choices.label: C
choices.text: A large pleural effusion expanding the hemithorax

choices.label: D
choices.text: Subcutaneous fat deposition over the chest wall

choices.label: E
choices.text: Pectus carinatum from costal cartilage overgrowth

explanation.summary: Loss of elastic recoil in emphysema traps air and raises residual volume, so the rib cage is held in a hyperinflated, expiratory-limited position. This increases the AP diameter, producing the barrel-shaped chest.
explanation.whyCorrect: Loss of elastic recoil in emphysema traps air and raises residual volume, so the rib cage is held in a hyperinflated, expiratory-limited position. This increases the AP diameter, producing the barrel-shaped chest.

questions.stem: This PA chest radiograph shows hyperlucent, hyperinflated lungs with flattened hemidiaphragms and a narrow vertical cardiac silhouette. These findings are most typical of which condition?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A reduced total exhaled volume that does not change with bronchodilator

choices.label: B
choices.text: A restrictive pattern with proportionally reduced FVC and FEV1

choices.label: C
choices.text: A faster-than-normal rise to a higher plateau

choices.label: D
choices.text: Slowed initial rise with FEV1 improving substantially after bronchodilator

choices.label: E
choices.text: An unchanged FEV1 before and after bronchodilator

explanation.summary: In asthma the volume-time curve rises slowly (airflow obstruction, low FEV1), and the dashed post-bronchodilator curve shows marked improvement toward normal, demonstrating reversibility, the hallmark distinguishing asthma from fixed obstruction.
explanation.whyCorrect: In asthma the volume-time curve rises slowly (airflow obstruction, low FEV1), and the dashed post-bronchodilator curve shows marked improvement toward normal, demonstrating reversibility, the hallmark distinguishing asthma from fixed obstruction.

questions.topicName: Asthma
questions.stem: On this bronchoprovocation test, the asthmatic curve reaches a 20% fall in FEV1 at a much lower inhaled agent dose than normal. What does this indicate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Reduced diffusing capacity of the lung

explanation.summary: A low PC20 (here 0.8 vs 20 mg/mL) means only a small provocative concentration of methacholine produces a 20% FEV1 drop, defining airway hyperresponsiveness characteristic of asthma.
explanation.whyCorrect: A low PC20 (here 0.8 vs 20 mg/mL) means only a small provocative concentration of methacholine produces a 20% FEV1 drop, defining airway hyperresponsiveness characteristic of asthma.

questions.topicName: Asthma
questions.stem: In the rightmost airway (asthmatic airway during an acute attack), which combination of changes is most responsible for the reduced airflow?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Accumulation of fluid within the alveoli only

choices.label: B
choices.text: Smooth muscle constriction plus wall inflammation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Loss of alveolar walls with permanent airspace enlargement

choices.label: D
choices.text: Thinning and dilation of the bronchial wall

choices.label: E
choices.text: Replacement of airway epithelium by fibrous scar with a fixed rigid lumen

explanation.summary: During an asthma attack bronchial smooth muscle contracts and the inflamed, thickened wall narrows the lumen, trapping air distally in alveoli. This bronchoconstriction plus inflammation is reversible, unlike the fixed destruction of emphysema.
explanation.whyCorrect: During an asthma attack bronchial smooth muscle contracts and the inflamed, thickened wall narrows the lumen, trapping air distally in alveoli. This bronchoconstriction plus inflammation is reversible, unlike the fixed destruction of emphysema.

questions.topicName: Treatment of Asthma & COPD
questions.stem: This mnemonic cartoon depicts a toxidrome of dry mouth, urinary retention, mydriasis, flushed hot skin, hyperthermia, tachycardia, confusion, and absent bowel sounds. Which inhaled COPD medication class can produce these systemic effects?

explanation.summary: The anticholinergic toxidrome (dry as a bone, red as a beet, hot as a desert, blind as a bat, mad as a hatter) results from muscarinic receptor blockade; inhaled antimuscarinics such as ipratropium and tiotropium used in COPD can cause these effects if systemically absorbed.
explanation.whyCorrect: The anticholinergic toxidrome (dry as a bone, red as a beet, hot as a desert, blind as a bat, mad as a hatter) results from muscarinic receptor blockade; inhaled antimuscarinics such as ipratropium and tiotropium used in COPD can cause these effects if systemically absorbed.

questions.topicName: Treatment of Asthma & COPD
questions.stem: This diagram shows the beta-agonist pathway (top right) increasing cAMP via adenylyl cyclase to promote bronchodilation. Which short-acting inhaled drug acts through this beta-receptor pathway for acute asthma relief?

explanation.summary: Albuterol is a short-acting beta-2 agonist that stimulates adenylyl cyclase to raise intracellular cAMP, relaxing bronchial smooth muscle; theophylline works instead by inhibiting phosphodiesterase, and ipratropium by blocking muscarinic receptors.
explanation.whyCorrect: Albuterol is a short-acting beta-2 agonist that stimulates adenylyl cyclase to raise intracellular cAMP, relaxing bronchial smooth muscle; theophylline works instead by inhibiting phosphodiesterase, and ipratropium by blocking muscarinic receptors.
